paras: The lynching of Elmo Curl was the hanging of Curl by a gathering of local men at Mastodon, Mississippi, in the summer of 1910. The Washington Herald described Curl as "a negro," and no paper reported what he was accused of. The case became known outside the South through a letter insisting that the hanging had been "a most orderly affair" carried out by the county's "best people," which northern and western papers reprinted and ridiculed in August and September 1910.

No direct news report of the hanging appears in the coverage; its details survive only in a letter quoted by editors elsewhere. According to the Springfield Republican, a newspaper correspondent had described the Mississippi mob as composed of ruffians, and Tax Assessor Miller of Concordia Parish, Louisiana, "just across the river from the place where the lynching took place," wrote to rebuke him. The Washington Herald, which did not name the writer, called him a citizen of Mastodon and quoted the nearby paper as calling the lynchers "a crazy, frenzied mob, composed of outlaws, thugs, and bums principally."

The letter said Curl had been hanged at Mastodon "last night" by the bankers, lawyers, farmers and merchants of the county, with no drinking, shooting, yelling or even loud talking. Its writer added that "all of the best people of that section took part," and the Washington Herald noted that he called himself a witness without admitting that he had joined in. The letter gave no date beyond "last night," and the earliest comment on it appeared on August 3, 1910.
No report of an arrest, inquest or official response appears in the coverage.

The Evening Times of Grand Forks, North Dakota, was the first paper found to comment, with an August 3 editorial headed "Orderly Murder" that wondered whether the letter writer had himself taken part and called the gathering "collective murder." On August 4 the Springfield Republican said the letter "deserves a place in the history of lynching in America," while the Washington Herald ran it under "A Very Polite Lynching" and closed by saying it opposed lynching "in any and all forms." The Fairmont West Virginian reprinted the Republican's item with credit on August 8.

A shorter version credited to "a Louisiana paper" changed "county" to "parish" and ran under the remark that the South was "proverbial" for good manners in the Abilene Weekly Reflector of Kansas on August 11 and the Emmett Index of Idaho on August 18. The Grand Forks Evening Times returned to the case on September 1, calling the lynching "a recent southern social event" and Miller "one of those present." All of the items found ran in white papers outside the South, and none was found in the Black press.

Accounts differ on who wrote the letter: the Springfield Republican and the Evening Times named Tax Assessor Miller of Concordia Parish, Louisiana, while the Washington Herald called the writer a citizen of Mastodon. The shorter squib presented the words as a Louisiana paper's own, writing "we" for "I," but the Republican's version, which names the writer and his office, is the more specific.

reader.title: Lynching of Elmo Curl
bases: Every account describes Curl as hanged at Mastodon, Miss., by an assembled body of local men and calls it a lynching (A2, A3, A8).

The letter quoted in A2 and A3 says the county's 'bankers, lawyers, farmers and merchants' met and hanged Curl, an extralegal killing by a large group; no accusation or motive is given, the victim's race appears only in A3, and all knowledge of the killing comes from one letter quoted in editorials, with no direct news report (A1, A2, A3).
Every item traces to one letter by a defender of the mob (A2, A3, A8); the nearby correspondent's report that prompted it is known only through these editorials (A2, A3).

framing.detail: Grand Forks Evening Times, 'Orderly Murder': calls the meeting 'collective murder' and wonders whether the writer took part.
Springfield Republican: says the letter 'deserves a place in the history of lynching in America'; ironic tone.
Washington Herald, 'A Very Polite Lynching': sarcastic; states it is opposed to lynching 'in any and all forms'.
Short squib under 'the south is proverbial for its good manners': quotes the letter with only a one-line ironic framing.
Grand Forks Evening Times, 'An Orderly Affair': calls the lynching 'a recent southern social event' in which Curl 'drew the first prize.'
